period_affected: Q2 2025, last 6 weeks (mid-May to end June)
weather_stated: close to 20% of Q2 operating days impacted by storms, rain and heat; 49 full park-closure days vs 12 in Q2 2024
impact_scope: combined system, last 6 weeks of Q2
quote: Over that six-week period, combined attendance was down 12% from the same timeframe last year, as severe storms, excessive rain, and extreme heat disrupted visitation and sales of season passes during the most critical portion of the sales cycle.
notes: weather_deviation is share of the QUARTER's operating days hit, not % above normal; share hit inside the 6-week window was higher. First 7 weeks (normal weather) were flat YoY, so ~12 pts is attributable to weather. Implied elasticity <=0.6 (12/20).

weather_stated: severe storms, excessive rain, extreme heat; 49 closure days vs 12
impact_metric: visits lost / profit margin on lost visits
quote: When we lose attendance, losing 1.4 million visitors over the last six weeks of the second quarter, that's all very high margin attendance lost. You're talking about attendance that's falling out, depending on the park, at a level that could be as high as 55%- 70% margin attendance
notes: Profit falls much more than revenue: lost visits carried 55-70% margin, i.e. only ~30-45% of lost revenue is offset by lower costs. Full-year 2025 EBITDA guide cut from $1.08-1.12bn to $860-910m (weather + pass base + consumer).

weather_stated: weather disruptions in May-June during pass sales season
quote: We lost a significant amount of passes, more than 300,000 season pass sales down in the months of May and June. You know, again, all sort of tied back to, you know, the weather disruptions that we spoke about.
notes: Pre-sold share does not fully insulate: bad weather in the selling window cuts pass sales themselves, which hurts the rest of the season. Mgmt called this 'the biggest and most significant headwind'.

weather_stated: extreme weather over seven weeks
quote: When you get extreme weather events like we had through those seven weeks when we were down significantly, you lose almost all your demand tickets, your one-day tickets.
notes: Single-day (walk-up) demand is nearly all lost on bad days; pass holders shift visits. Supports applying the weather loss mainly to the non-pass share.

weather_stated: extreme weather conditions coupled with economic uncertainty
deferred_or_lost: mixed (mgmt says delayed; H2 guide cut implies mostly lost)
quote: we believe many guests delayed park visits during the early weeks of our operating season, making fewer impulse buys, delaying purchases of season passes and memberships, and displaying a more value-conscious mindset.
notes: Mgmt framed it as delay, but July attendance was only +1% (revenue -3%) and FY EBITDA guidance was cut ~$215m at midpoint, so recapture was small. Treat as mostly lost.

weather_stated: Hurricane Beryl, record heat and rain across much of North America; several parks forced to close
quote: Over the five-week period ended August 4, 2024, attendance across the combined portfolio totaled 10.9 million visits, down 3% or approximately 350,000 visits compared to the same five-week period last year.
notes: CEO: attendance was down only 1% at parks not forced to close (https://web.quartr.com/m/sources/s77696079289140968946552), so ~2 pts came from closures. No day-count given.

weather_stated: unusually high rainfall in the Northeast plus record heat wave in the South
quote: The, the weather hedge, the, the weather impact on our, on our Q2 really feels like somewhere between five and six points of, of lost attendance.
notes: Midpoint of 5-6 pts. Q2 attendance was 7.1m (+6% YoY). No % of days given.

weather_stated: poor weather (Northeast rain, Southern heat)
quote: Our F&B is up despite poor weather. We lost in Q almost 400,000 in attendance.
notes: 400k / (7.1m + 0.4m) = 5.3%. Same call: 'We do not expect to make up weather-related losses.' (https://web.quartr.com/m/sources/s70760277165595992636445).

weather_stated: spring rain in California, record summer heat in Texas, eight consecutive rainy weekends in Mid-Atlantic/Northeast after Labor Day
quote: We estimate that adverse weather reduced full-year attendance by over 1 million guests. This includes rain and snow in California during spring break, followed by a record summer heat wave in Texas, and eight consecutive weekends of rain or threat of rain in the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast
notes: >1.0m / (22.2m actual + 1.0m) = ~4.3% of normal attendance. Mixed perils (rain + heat), not all May-Sep.

weather_stated: unusually cold and rainy weather; baseline = 5-year average attendance ex-2020
quote: we experienced unusually cold and rainy weather in California and Texas during the quarter, which we estimate accounted for a loss of 180,000 in attendance based on a five-year average attendance excluding 2020.
notes: 180k / (1.6m + 0.18m) = 10%. Out of the May-Sep season (spring); a low-volume quarter, so % loss is large. Use with care.

weather_stated: unusually hot and cold weather, rain, Canadian wildfire smoke
quote: The decrease in attendance was primarily due to significantly adverse weather, including some combination of unusually hot and cold weather, rain, and/or the fallout from Canadian wildfires across most of our markets, including during peak visitation periods.
notes: Revenue -1.7% (per-cap +0.3%). Also some impact from ride-opening timing. Raw YoY, not a weather estimate.

weather_stated: unusual heat and/or rain across most markets in peak periods
quote: The decrease in attendance was primarily due to significantly adverse weather, including some combination of unusual heat and/or rain across most of our markets, including during peak visitation periods.
notes: Revenue -3.0%, per-cap -0.2%. CEO: without weather 'I don't know that we would have been positive, but ... a lot closer' (https://web.quartr.com/m/sources/s350077565599738602362).

weather_stated: Hurricanes Debby (Aug) and Helene (Sep) plus a negative calendar shift
quote: The combined impact of the calendar shift and the meaningfully worse weather was approximately 320,000 guests. Adjusting for these impacts, attendance would have increased approximately 3% compared to the prior year quarter.
notes: Actual -1.4% (-100k) vs adjusted +3% => ~4.4 pts, but this INCLUDES a calendar shift (mostly July), so weather alone is less. Revenue only -0.4% thanks to per-cap +1.0%.

weather_stated: Hurricanes Debby, Helene and Milton
quote: We estimate that the combined impact of the meaningfully worse weather was approximately 167,000 guests in the fourth quarter and 432,000 guests for the fiscal year.
notes: Q4 attendance -1.6% (-79k) actual vs ~+2% weather-adjusted; 167k/(~4.86m+0.167m)=3.3-3.4%. FY: 432k guests, mgmt says FY would have been ~+2%. Hurricanes, not ordinary rainy days.

weather_stated: Hurricane Ian
quote: We had a meaningful impact from adverse weather in the quarter, including Hurricane Ian, that we estimate led to 90,000 less guest visits during the quarter.
notes: No denominator stated in this paragraph; % not computed.

weather_stated: wildfire smoke, excessive heat, untimely and extended rain
quote: This poor weather, not surprisingly, impacted our attendance in the month. Fortunately, though, we saw good admissions and in-park per capita growth during the month. Our preliminary view has revenue being down approximately 2% in the month of July.
notes: Preliminary; per-cap growth offset part of the attendance loss.

weather_stated: significantly unfavorable weather plus calendar and international headwinds
quote: Excluding the impact of these unusual headwinds, which amounted to approximately 325,000 visits, our attendance would have been up.
notes: Attendance -320k (-4.7%) but revenue only -1.1% because per-cap +3.8% (https://web.quartr.com/m/sources/s80762551634767484004387). 325k mixes weather, calendar and international; not separable.

region: Illinois (Raging Waves) and other US water parks
weather_stated: June cooler than normal with rainfall well above normal
quote: Raging Waves, our 54-acre waterpark outside Chicago, saw attendance fall significantly against a June that ran cooler than normal with rainfall well above normal.
notes: CFO: water parks were 'about $3 million-$5 million of incremental weather' (https://web.quartr.com/m/sources/s354723224724743930306); -4m is the midpoint, not a stated figure. Water parks TTM revenue to July ~$56m. CEO now calls season passes 'weather insurance'.

weather_stated: rain closed the outdoor water park on opening day
quote: The first day Raging Waves was supposed to open, it actually didn't open because of rain, and what we found is in the three districts that comprise the centers in the Chicago area, we were up about 90% same-store sales versus prior year.
notes: Inverse effect: indoor venues gain on rainy days and are 'very challenged' on good-weather days. Single-day anecdote; do not use as an elasticity.

weather_stated: authorities forced festival shutdowns due to extreme heat
quote: There have been cancellations, as you quite rightly pointed out. All our events are fully insured. There was no negative impact in Q2 from those cancellations.
notes: Revenue lost but insured, so net earnings impact ~0. Heat (not rain) closures of outdoor events; analyst description at https://web.quartr.com/m/sources/s89159542798160632452705.

region: US central regions (~40% of Lennox revenue)
weather_stated: cooling degree days down >30% and precipitation up >60% in key central regions
quote: Our residential business in the second quarter was negatively impacted by the significantly cooler temperatures and higher precipitation across the U.S., especially in key central regions where cooling degree days were down more than 30% and precipitation was up more than 60%
notes: CDD % is vs prior year, regional. Segment revenue $689m, -4%, despite +3.6% price; includes tornado (factory) loss of $28m.

weather_stated: cool, wet Q2 (CDD -30% in central regions)
quote: The larger number in the quarter is weather, and that's by definition, it's weather, and it's 100% weather.
notes: Same paragraph: tornado impact was $28m in the quarter. Lower bound: weather loss > $28m = >3.9% of prior-year segment revenue (~$718m). If it sat in the central regions (40% of revenue), that is >~10% regional loss vs CDD -30% => regional elasticity >=~0.33; likely 0.4-0.6 once price growth is netted. impact_usd is the lower bound.

region: US (Lennox-branded, centre of country vs Allied)
weather_stated: cool weather concentrated in centre of country
impact_scope: Lennox direct (80% of revenue) vs Allied/ADP
quote: Our direct business, our Lennox business, which is 80% of what we do revenue-wise, is down 6%. Our Allied and ADP businesses, which are direct, was up 3%. I think it's a couple things. I think it's weather exposure. Our Lennox branded business is more in the center of the country
notes: ~9 pt gap between centre-exposed and other brands; partly weather, partly share loss after tornado.

weather_stated: warm weather in Florida
quote: in a market like Florida where we had warm weather, our Lennox replacement revenue was up 12%.
notes: Contrast case: same quarter, warm region up strongly. No CDD figure given.

weather_stated: cooling degree days up 9% vs prior year
quote: Sort of on the flip side, you look at a state like Texas, cooling degree days were up 9% in Q3, and our revenue was up 10%.
notes: Elasticity ~1.1 (10/9), hot-side, one state, raw YoY (includes price and share).

weather_stated: CDD down ~5% nationally; down ~10% in swing regions in July-August
quote: It's hard to know, Robert. We didn't even do that, and I don't think we did that in the second quarter. Net, it was degree cooling days were down about 5% or so for the quarter, and especially in the swing areas, that's where it hurt us.
notes: Mgmt declined to size the weather hit. Segment revenue +7% (easy tornado comp), so not usable for elasticity. Swing-region detail: https://web.quartr.com/m/sources/s62992569968706466155280.

weather_stated: CDD +4% for Q2 and +12% in June vs prior year
quote: Our residential business improved each month through the quarter and was up 7% in June as the economy continued to reopen and weather heated up for the summer. Cooling degree days for the second quarter overall were up 4% from the prior year quarter.
notes: June CDD +12% (same paragraph). Naive elasticity ~0.6 but confounded by COVID reopening; low weight.

weather_stated: cooler start to summer; June 'a little colder'
quote: Now, you gotta ignore things like weather, because June was a little colder, July is gonna be a little bit harder, but that just get washes out for the full year, Tommy.
notes: Volume -12% was mostly distributor destocking per CEO; weather share not sized (https://web.quartr.com/m/sources/s54892729914938402305948). Key point: OEM sees a cool June as timing that washes out over the year.

weather_stated: May 'coldest May in 20+ years' per anecdotal data; late start to summer
quote: May was very soft. Towards the end of June, we saw much stronger sales. Yes, there's clearly a pattern that's related to weather.
notes: Not quantified; refrigerant transition and destocking also in play. Demand shifted later rather than vanished (June/July strength).

weather_stated: CDD down 23% vs prior year, lowest in 10 years
quote: This was driven by a 23% decline in Cooling Degree Days versus the prior year period to the lowest level in 10 years. We also saw a similar decline in our HVAC claims due to cooler than normal weather.
notes: impact_pct is approximate: mgmt said a 'similar decline' to the 23% CDD drop. Implies HVAC repair call volume ~1:1 with CDD. $17m is Frontdoor's claims-cost BENEFIT, i.e. revenue lost by repair contractors. Repair calls on a cool summer are mostly lost (unit didn't fail).

weather_stated: CDD up 20% vs prior year
quote: We anticipated a higher number of service requests in HVAC, given the large favorability we saw in the second quarter of 2023, driven by mild weather, and that is what happened as cooling degree days increased 20%. However, we only saw a moderate increase in the HVAC incidence rate
notes: Asymmetry: +20% CDD gave only a 'moderate' rise in HVAC calls (also fee changes, member geography). Suggests elasticity well below 1 on the hot side for this book; ~0.2-0.5.

weather_stated: CDD down 16% vs prior year
quote: First, we had $14 million of favorable weather, as cooling degree days were down 16% versus the prior year period.
notes: Dollar benefit to Frontdoor = repair work not done by contractors. Claims base not given in this paragraph, so no %.

weather_stated: arrival of hot weather delayed; decline in cooling degree days
quote: As we mentioned, beyond the tough comps and supply chain issues, the arrival of a hot summer weather was delayed this year, as evidenced by the decline in cooling degree days.
notes: Not sized; supply-chain impact ($75-80m) dominated the quarter.

weather_stated: weak weather in first half, then heat
quote: Seeing a, an uptick, which, you know, because the weather was so weak in the first half of the year, we're seeing an uptick in repair parts, which is always good for us on a gross profit basis.
notes: Evidence of catch-up once heat arrives: some cool-period demand is deferred, not lost.

weather_stated: cooler, wetter June in certain markets
quote: sales and earnings strength during the first two months of the quarter were disrupted in June by cooler, wet-wetter weather, and that's something, wetter weather in certain markets. July growth trends have improved
notes: Weakness concentrated in central US; Florida grew. Not sized.

weather_stated: weak May in the north
quote: Where the weather really impacts us is up north where we've got, you know, where it's, you've got a chance out of every third year that you're going to have a hotter than normal summer or a normal summer or a lower than normal summer.
notes: Regional point: Florida/Texas demand is weather-insensitive ('always hot'); northern markets swing with summer heat. Implies the elasticity should be applied mainly to temperate/northern locations.

weather_stated: CDD 'not really on target', especially May-June
quote: We had degree cooling days that were not really on target for the entire year, especially the peak part of the year, which is May and June, when people are thinking about putting in a new air conditioner, but if the weather doesn't get hot, they don't.
notes: Replacement decisions are postponed when early summer is cool; not sized. 2025 also had refrigerant transition and weak housing.

weather_stated: US CDD up ~4%; heat in Europe
quote: Clearly, cooling degree days, we don't like to get into the weather. They were, I think, up something like 4%. The heat did help, not only here, but in places like Europe. Europe, we saw air conditioning orders up 20%, which will position us as we go here into 3Q.
notes: The 4% CDD is US; Europe's weather deviation not given, so no elasticity. Orders, not revenue.

weather_stated: CDD softer than usual in last six weeks of Q2
quote: Cooling degree days was softer in the last six weeks of the quarter than usual. Having said that, the weather is the weather, but what really happened was movement was softer in June in particular.
notes: Not sized; mgmt blames rates/consumer too.

weather_stated: prolonged cool weather until mid-June
quote: refrigerant sales volume was slightly lower than last year due to a late start to the summer weather in the Northeast and Midwest. This was partially offset by an increase in the average selling price of refrigerants.
notes: Service-driven demand (first hot days trigger repair calls). Volume recovered from mid-June. Price offset part.

weather_stated: nationwide heat wave, 'extremely hot in multiple areas'
quote: From an impact on the business, I would say very little. We want to make sure our, our employees are safe. And, you know, as you think about productivity on a job, you know, the most important thing to us is safety.
notes: Mgmt: heat impact 'very little'; extra breaks only. Contrast: rain earlier caused real disruption (https://web.quartr.com/m/sources/s349263971175049251510).

weather_stated: hot summer vs earlier California rains
quote: This isn't the same kind of disruption. You know, this kind of heat isn't, isn't really creating the same kind of disruption that the, those rainfall issues were creating earlier on.
notes: Heat is a much smaller disruption than rain for crews paid by the job.

weather_stated: extreme heat in Arizona and the Southwest
quote: We have our crews starting much earlier and working up to the point where they can. We're getting full days in right now, by starting much earlier and, you know, finishing earlier in the day as well before the heat peaks out.
notes: Hours shifted earlier, not lost ('full days in'). No revenue effect stated.

weather_stated: extreme heat
quote: You may not be as productive in those times when that heat is extreme like that, but usually, that goes on for weeks, not months.
notes: Some productivity loss on hottest weeks, not sized.

weather_stated: high temperatures in the Southwest
quote: For renewable energy work, we didn't grow in the quarter due to the lower volume on existing solar projects, mainly driven by high temperatures in the Southwest United States, as well as delayed new project starts.
notes: Only call found tying heat to lost billable hours for day-labour; not sized and mixed with project delays.

weather_stated: extreme heat wave plus election-related labour shortage
quote: Hopefully, I think the Q2 conditions is far more better than what we have seen in Q1, because Q1 we had the twin problems of shortage of labor due to elections and also extreme heat.
notes: Heat and elections not separated. Mgmt kept full-year guidance (execution shifted to H2), so mostly deferred for the firm; for daily-paid workers hours were lost.

weather_stated: several days of extreme temperatures (day-after-day >35C mentioned in same call)
quote: At the end of June, the outside temperatures were so extreme for our colleagues for several days that we had to put the heat protocol into effect for a prolonged period, a situation that we expect to occur more often in the coming years.
notes: CEO raised possibility of a formal 'extreme heat' leave scheme like the cold-weather one. Not sized.

weather_stated: extreme heat and humidity at peak construction season
quote: At Badger, we manage these exposures with regular hydration, cooling off breaks, and job sharing rotations to ensure the safety and productivity of our team members.
notes: Same call reports double-digit revenue growth; no heat loss stated.

weather_stated: increased heat
quote: With increased heat, the weather challenges in different geographies. We just saw much higher absenteeism over there. And when that happens, you obviously have to bring in people with much lower dexterity levels. And that means productivity gets impacted.
notes: Absenteeism = lost days for the absent workers. Not sized.
